name: Humanist sans
region: England, later Germany and the United States
summary: A sans serif on the skeleton of the Renaissance roman: open apertures, varied widths, a little stroke modulation and an angled cut on the terminals. It reads well at small sizes and in poor conditions, and sounds warm.

philosophy.core_thesis: A sans serif reads best when it keeps the proportions and the open forms of the written roman.
design_principles: Open the apertures of c, e, a and s: the gap of the c is at least 0.35 of its height.
Keep a slight stroke modulation of 1.1–1.6:1, with thinner joins where curves meet stems.
Cut the terminals at an angle, as a pen stroke ends.
Give the letters classical widths: a wide O and M, a narrow E, S and r.
Hold the x-height at 0.66–0.78 of the cap height.
Use a true italic with cursive forms, not a sloped roman.
anti_patterns: Pure geometric circles for o and a single-storey a
A sloped roman as the italic
Very tight tracking in text sizes

classification.note: A humanist sans takes its proportions from the roman capital and the Renaissance minuscule; a geometric sans takes them from the circle and the square.

anatomy.contrast: Slight: the thin parts are 0.65–0.9 of the stem.
anatomy.serifs: None: the strokes end clean, with no serif.
anatomy.terminals: Angled cuts on c, e, s, a and t.
anatomy.aperture: Open: the c, e and s have wide mouths, and the bowl of the e is clearly separated from its tail.
anatomy.key_letters: A two-storey a and often a two-storey g, an l with a tail in some faces, and a true cursive italic.

metrics.x_height: The x-height is 0.66–0.78 of the cap height and about 0.46–0.53 of the em.
metrics.contrast: The side of the o is 1.0 to 1.6 times as thick as its top.
metrics.width: Varied, classical widths; the mean advance of a to z is 0.44–0.52 em.
metrics.figures: Lining or old-style figures, often both in one family.

setting.text_sizes: Set text at 9–11 pt in print and 14–17 px on screen; it also holds at 11–12 px for captions.
setting.display_sizes: Set titles at 24–96 px in semibold or bold.
setting.leading: Set the leading at 1.4–1.6 for text and 1.1–1.2 for titles.
setting.tracking: Set 0 em in text, −0.01 em in large titles, and +0.05 em for capitals.
setting.case_and_features: Use the true italic for emphasis, small caps where the family has them, and old-style figures in running text.

pairing.rule: Pair it with a serif that shares the pen-based skeleton, so both faces have the same rhythm.

pairs.why: The humanist sans is a Garalde without serifs, so the proportions agree.
A humanist slab keeps the open forms and adds weight for titles.

faces.designer: Erik Spiekermann and Carrois for Mozilla

reference_faces.note: Fira Sans and Source Sans are new designs in the class, not revivals of one face. The default instance of Source Sans 3 in google/fonts is ExtraLight, so the specimen uses Fira Sans Regular.

emotion.target_response: Warm clarity: the reader feels a friendly, human voice that is still modern and easy to read.

use_cases: product interfaces with a warm voice
avoid_when: The brief asks for a strict, neutral grid voice.
The brief asks for a geometric, avant-garde look.

modifiers.how: Close the apertures with horizontal terminals and even the widths; keep the x-height.
Add bracketed serifs and raise the contrast to 2.5:1; keep the proportions.

sources.title: Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style (Hartley & Marks, 4th ed. 2012)
